Location

Mag Point

A fading fishing town on the edge of the Alaskan wilderness, where rugged mountains, icy waters, and dense coastal fog have shaped life for over two centuries. Since the late 1980s, the Gray Signal has been bleeding through Mag Point, forever entwining the town with a string of unexplained disappearances and mysteries that continue to haunt its residents.

RegionSoutheast Alaska, Baranof Island
Population9,942 and falling
Founded1805
StatusGray signal active

The town

“The first thing you’ll notice about Mag Point is the fog. The last thing you’ll remember is what you saw inside it.”

Mag Point is a remote coastal town on Baranof Island in Southeast Alaska, a place where civilization ends and the wilderness begins. Wedged between towering mountain ridges and the icy waters of the Gulf of Alaska, it spends much of the year beneath heavy clouds, relentless rain, and endless winter nights. Sunshine is a rare luxury reserved for the brief summer months. Thick coastal fog drifts in from the sea throughout the year, but in August it becomes almost unnatural, blanketing the town and surrounding forests for days at a time. Once a thriving fishing and oil town, Mag Point has spent decades in slow decline. Young people leave in search of a better future, businesses struggle to survive, and abandoned buildings stand as reminders of more prosperous days. The town has earned a grim reputation among outsiders.

Since the late 1980s, Mag Point has been plagued by a series of unexplained disappearances. Many dismiss them as unfortunate accidents caused by the unforgiving Alaskan wilderness or attribute them to the nearby Alaska Triangle, a region infamous for mysterious vanishings and unsolved cases. The greatest tragedy came in August 2008, when five young children vanished within days of one another, shattering the community. A decade later, in 2018, the disappearances begin again, drawing investigators into a mystery that reaches far beyond missing persons. In this story, Mag Point is more than a setting. It is a character in its own right: a lonely, weather-beaten town where every August the fog returns, bringing with it questions no one has ever been able to answer.

History of Mag Pointopen file

The Russian Frontier (1805–1867)

Mag Point was founded in 1805 by Russian explorer Vasiliy Sokolov. Originally known as Fort Mag Point, it served as the easternmost military and trading outpost of the Russian-American Company on Baranof Island. The settlement occupied a narrow strip of land between steep mountain ridges and the sea, making it both naturally protected and strategically important. Ships departing from its harbor carried explorers, hunters, missionaries, and supplies deeper into the Alaskan frontier. The fort remained small but prosperous, becoming known for its skilled shipwrights, fisheries, and timber trade.


Under American Rule (1867–1897)

Following the United States’ purchase of Alaska in 1867, Mag Point peacefully transitioned to American administration. Many Russian settlers remained, leaving behind an architectural and cultural legacy still visible throughout the town. The harbor continued to grow as a regional shipping stop, while fishing gradually replaced the fur trade as the town’s primary industry.


The Gold Rush Boom (1897–1915)

Although no major gold deposits were discovered near Mag Point itself, the town became an important supply port during the Klondike Gold Rush. Hotels, warehouses, saloons, banks, and shipping companies appeared almost overnight as thousands of prospectors passed through on their way north. At its peak, Mag Point was one of southeastern Alaska’s busiest coastal settlements. When the Gold Rush ended, many newcomers stayed, helping transform the temporary frontier town into a permanent community.


A Fishing Town (1915–1929)

With mining in decline, Mag Point embraced commercial fishing. Large canneries, shipyards, and seafood processing facilities were built along the waterfront, while schools, churches, parks, and civic buildings reshaped the growing town. The original Russian fort was dismantled during this period, with only a monument to its founder, Vasiliy Sokolov, remaining in the town square.


Decline and Recovery (1929–1970)

The Great Depression severely affected Mag Point. Businesses closed, unemployment soared, and many families left in search of work elsewhere. The town slowly recovered after World War II as military contracts, improved infrastructure, and renewed fishing activity brought jobs back to the region. New roads, neighborhoods, and public buildings modernized much of the aging settlement.


Oil and Prosperity (1970–1990)

The discovery of offshore oil led to another economic boom. “Shoreside Petroleum” established operations near Mag Point, creating hundreds of jobs alongside the already thriving fishing industry. By the early 1980s, the population had reached nearly 25,000, making Mag Point one of the largest towns in southeastern Alaska. Modern schools, a hospital, expanded harbor facilities, and private businesses reflected the town’s newfound prosperity. Yet during the late 1970s, a handful of unusual events began to circulate among locals. Hunters occasionally reported strange lights deep in the mountains. Fishermen described hearing distant voices over calm waters where no boats were present. Unexplained radio interference was dismissed as a natural anomaly, becoming little more than local folklore.


Modern Times (1990–now)

By the early 1990s, Mag Point entered a long period of economic decline. Fish stocks became less reliable, oil production slowed, and many of the town’s largest employers began reducing their workforce. Younger generations left for larger Alaskan cities or the mainland in search of better opportunities.

By 2008, the population had fallen from nearly 25,000 to approximately 15,000, leaving Mag Point struggling to preserve its identity. Around the same time, unsettling rumors began to spread. A handful of unexplained disappearances that had started in the late Cold War years became more frequent, though never numerous enough to attract national attention. Local authorities investigated each case individually, attributing them to accidents, harsh wilderness conditions, or people leaving town without notice. Among residents, however, whispers persisted that something darker had taken root in Mag Point.

Despite its decline, the town remains alive. Its harbor still served a modest fishing fleet, “Shoreside Petroleum” maintained regional operations, and family-owned businesses fought to survive alongside aging hotels, restaurants, and seafood processing facilities. To outsiders, Mag Point was simply another struggling Alaskan coastal town.

To its residents, it was a place that had never quite let go of its past.

The map

Click a pin marker to open that location. Each one carries its own photos, notes, items, quests, and encounters that you will experience during the gameplay.

Town Center

Mag Point Center is the town's most well-maintained district. At its heart lies Washington Square, featuring a monument dedicated to Vasiliy Sokolov, the founder of Fort Mag Point. The location has hotel and bed-and-breakfast, pubs and bars, a popular pizzeria "The Fisherman's Daughter", the police station, the Museum of Alaskan History, the City Library, a Lutheran church, and a variety of privately owned shops and businesses.


In STATIC, Mag Point Center serves as the game's primary hub. Here, players can safely explore the streets, save their progress, speak with locals, collect and inspect clues, and advance their investigations with assistance from the town's police department. However, when darkness falls over Mag Point, the town center is no longer as safe as it seems. Players may notice changes in the behavior of their allies and discover places and pathways that weren't there before.

Big Bear Bay

The industrial port of Mag Point, Big Bear Bay is where the town earns its living from the sea. Three weather-beaten piers, an aging fishing cannery, rusting trawlers, and several waterfront pubs. The air is heavy with the smell of salt, diesel, fish, and rotting seaweed. Dense coastal fog clings to the docks almost year-round, swallowing ships and muffling every sound. By day, sailors, fishermen, and dockworkers gather here, and many of them know Ian well enough to offer information or a helping hand. Saoirse, however, is regarded with suspicion: outsiders are never fully trusted in Mag Point.


In STATIC, the harbor becomes one of the town's most dangerous places after dark. The Gray Signal is unusually strong here, warping familiar surroundings into something deeply unsettling. The maze of docks, warehouses, and abandoned vessels turns into hostile territory where every shadow feels alive. Exploring Big Bear Bay at night is rarely a good idea, but sometimes it's the only way to uncover the truth or save someone before it's too late.

Outskirts

The Outskirts are a run-down waterfront district bordering Big Bear Bay, where abandoned houses, rusting cars, and neglected streets paint a picture of a town in steady decline. Cheap rent has made the neighborhood home to drifters, addicts, alcoholics, and troublemakers. Despite its reputation, this is where Ian lives.


In STATIC, the Outskirts serve as Ian's resources location, allowing him to return home to restock supplies and stimulants before venturing back into main quest. This area is hostile for both protagonists, but Ian can find a helping hand and extra clues if the player decides to explore the location thoroughly. The district also plays a major role in the story: Saoirse must eventually navigate its hostile streets on her own, and in the final act, the protagonists gather here before setting out on their last journey beyond the borders of Mag Point.

Old Docks

Hidden beyond the forest on the outskirts of Mag Point, the Old Docks are all that remains of a long-abandoned private industrial site. A crumbling pier, rusted warehouses, and wooden shacks slowly decay beneath the coastal fog, cut off from the rest of the town by dense woodland. Once operated by a private company, the area was sealed off from the public. Old Docks is where the Gray Signal activity is at it's pick. People, lured here by the Operator, were never seen again.


In STATIC, the Old Docks are the most dangerous location in the game. The Operator saturates the area with its projections designed to deceive, isolate, and lure intruders deeper into its domain. Here you may discover a hidden bunker entrance if the game gives you an oppurtunity to do so. Failing to discover it leads to an entirely different ending.

Residents

The residential block is the quiet heart of everyday life in Mag Point. Neat family homes with trimmed lawns, white picket fences, and narrow streets create the image of a peaceful neighborhood. Small grocery stores, convenience shops, playgrounds, and family-owned businesses serve the local community. Ian's parents and his younger brother, Victor, live here, making the district one of the most personal locations in the story.


In STATIC, that sense of comfort disappears after sunset. Most residents remain behind locked doors, and anyone wandering the streets may not be who they appear to be. The Gray Signal gives rise to doppelgangers that are nearly indistinguishable from real people, forcing you to rely on conversation and observation before deciding whether to trust or confront them. Resources are scarce in the residential block, making preparation essential before venturing into the neighborhood at night.

Commercial Block

Once envisioned as the business center of Mag Point, the Commercial Block is now a quiet district of aging office buildings, small businesses, and mostly empty parking lots. Many companies have downsized or left town altogether, leaving entire floors vacant and gathering dust. The largest building belongs to "Shoreside Petroleum", the regional oil company where Ian works. Despite the district's decline, a handful of offices, government services, and local businesses continue to operate.


In STATIC, the Commercial Block remains one of the few locations that is relatively safe both day and night. Even so, the Gray Signal occasionally seeps into the empty hallways and darkened offices, producing fleeting sights and sounds that defy explanation. Although the story only brings you here twice, careful exploration can uncover useful supplies, documents, and equipment that make later expeditions into Mag Point's more dangerous districts a bit easier.

Forest

Stretching between Mag Point and the Old Docks, the Forest is a dense expanse of towering spruce, tangled undergrowth, and narrow trails that seem to disappear into the fog. Sunlight rarely reaches the forest floor, and the deeper you venture, the quieter everything becomes. Fallen trees and abandoned hunting cabins hint at lives that once passed through these woods, but few people willingly enter them anymore.


In STATIC, the Forest is the only route to the Old Docks and, ultimately, to the Operator. It is also one of the game's most psychologically dangerous locations. The Gray Signal distorts your sense of direction, making it easy to become lost. Ian's mental state steadily deteriorates when he enters this area. Scattered throughout the woods are mysterious artifacts connected to the Operator and the Gray Signal. Some guide you forward, others deliberately lure you away from your destination. Deciding which signs to trust is essential for survival.

White High School

"White High School" is where Ian and Saiorse both studied ten years ago. They were high school sweethearts, bound together by a shared sense of escape from the town around them. Ian holds onto those memories with quiet attachment, while Saoirse regards them with resentment, treating her past as something she has long since tried to leave behind.


In STATIC, "White High School" functions as a narrative anchor through flashbacks that contrast sharply with the present-day decay of Mag Point. Collectible items found here resonate with the current timeline, unlocking new perspectives, memories, or potential directions for the investigation. These sequences not only provide brief moments of warmth and clarity, but also give hints which players can use in the main storyline.
